title: The Gang Reignites the Rivalry

jokes.text: Frank wearing skinny jeans, the gang reacts in horror
jokes.setup: Frank wants to stay young and hip, so he's wearing skinny jeans
jokes.punchline: Frank's stocky, older body in skinny jeans — described as a 'Humpty Dumpty vibe' — is visually absurd and antithetical to what skinny jeans are supposed to do
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank vanity gag. Works because it's perfectly in character — Frank desperately wants to be young and cool — and the visual of a short, squat older man in skinny jeans is inherently funny. The 'Humpty Dumpty' descriptor elevates it from pure visual to a solid craft moment.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I like 'em. I think they make me look sexy.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is telling Frank he looks ridiculous
jokes.punchline: Frank doubles down with total sincerity that the jeans make him look sexy
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of self-awareness is his defining trait. Saying 'I think they make me look sexy' with complete conviction after universal mockery is perfectly in character. The economy is excellent — four words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I am getting a tremendous amount of enjoyment watching you parade around in those things. So I say keep them.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It's like a Humpty Dumpty vibe going on with those.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been watching Frank parade around
jokes.punchline: The 'Humpty Dumpty' comparison is specific, cruel, and perfectly visual
jokes.explanation: The Humpty Dumpty comparison is a genuinely good joke — specific enough to be memorable, economical, and cruel in the precise way Dennis is cruel. It paints an excellent picture without being gratuitous.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Big news, bitches! The ban's been lifted. And we are back in. Flipadelphia, here we come!

jokes.text: Mac's 'Yo-oh! Big news, bitches!' entrance and the gang's immediate pivot to Flipadelphia excitement
jokes.setup: The gang is in the middle of mocking Frank's pants
jokes.punchline: Mac bursts in with over-the-top energy about a city-wide flip cup tournament, instantly making the pants irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Standard gang-energy gag. The pivot works because of their collective enthusiasm for something utterly trivial. 'Big news, bitches!' is functional character-voice work.

dialogue.line: Flip, flip, Flipadelphia!

jokes.text: The entire gang chanting 'Flip, flip, Flipadelphia!' with tremendous enthusiasm
jokes.setup: Mac announces the city-wide flip cup tournament
jokes.punchline: The gang explodes into a ridiculous, synchronized chant about flip cup as if it's the most important thing in the world
jokes.explanation: The chant is immediately iconic within the episode and becomes a running gag. The disproportionate enthusiasm for a bar game is perfect Always Sunny — these people treat flip cup with the gravity of a war campaign. High quotability; it's the kind of thing viewers adopt.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, we did poison the shit out of them. But they didn't have any proof.

jokes.text: Mac explaining they 'very, very unfairly' accused the gang of poisoning a rival team, then immediately: 'No, we did poison the shit out of them. But they didn't have any proof.'
jokes.setup: Mac frames the past accusation as deeply unfair
jokes.punchline: He immediately and casually admits they absolutely did it, with zero remorse
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes structurally. The setup 'very, very unfairly accused' primes the audience to expect a wrongful-accusation story, then the instant reversal — 'No, we did poison the shit out of them' — is perfectly timed. It's a textbook misdirection with a genuinely dark twist, and the 'but they didn't have any proof' adds a legal-procedural absurdity that's pure Always Sunny. The structure is excellent and it sets up the entire episode's premise.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This year we're gonna jam it right up their butt holes...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, me, Dennis and Charlie will jam their butt holes.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Yeah, yeah. This year we're gonna jam it right up their butt holes.' Dennis: 'Ohh! Wow. Yeah, me, Dennis and Charlie will jam their butt holes.'
jokes.setup: Mac is talking about beating their rivals at flip cup
jokes.punchline: The 'butt hole' metaphor is delivered with such specific earnestness that Dennis enthusiastically repeats it verbatim, unaware of how it sounds
jokes.explanation: Juvenile but functional. The joke is in the earnestness with which they discuss 'butt holes' as a competitive strategy. Not particularly clever but consistent with the show's texture.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're not gonna come anywhere near their butt holes. Let us handle the butt holes.

jokes.text: Mac to Dee: 'You're not gonna come anywhere near their butt holes. Let us handle the butt holes.'
jokes.setup: Dee wants to be on the flip cup team
jokes.punchline: Mac's exclusion of Dee gets filtered through the butt hole language, making the gatekeeping even more absurd
jokes.explanation: The butt hole language extended to exclude Dee is a decent callback within the same scene. Works primarily because of the absurdity of the phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm your 'Adelphia.'

jokes.text: Dee: 'I'm your number four. I'm your Adelphia.'
jokes.setup: The gang is debating whether Dee should be on the flip cup team
jokes.punchline: Dee pathetically argues she is literally the last syllable of 'Flipadelphia' — 'Adelphia' — as a reason to include her
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. Dee's desperation to be included manifests as a wordplay justification — she is literally 'Adelphia,' the fourth part of the chant. It's pathetic, funny, and very character-specific to Dee's perpetual exclusion from the group.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You choked under pressure in '98. You blew the whole thing. We were gonna win. And then you couldn't flip your damn cup over.

jokes.text: The gang arrives to taunt their rival bar Molly's and finds it's been beautifully renovated
jokes.setup: The gang confidently refers to Molly's as a 'shithole' and enters expecting to intimidate
jokes.punchline: It's a lovely, busy restaurant — their posturing immediately deflates
jokes.explanation: A structural joke that sets up the gang's obliviousness. Their confidence about the bar being a dive is immediately undermined. Functional setup-deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Flip cup. Ten years ago? We poisoned you, dude. Remember?

jokes.text: Mac crashing into Molly's yelling 'Guess who, bitches!' then squeaking 'Oh, yeah! Whoo!' over diners' food, honking and chanting 'Eat it! Eat it!'
jokes.setup: The gang is supposed to be intimidating their rivals; they're in a nice restaurant full of normal diners
jokes.punchline: Their taunting — honking horns, chanting 'eat it' at strangers eating — is horrifyingly inappropriate given the upscale context
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cringe — the gang's completely inappropriate behavior in a normal social setting. The specificity of 'honk honk honk' and 'eat it eat it' chanted at dining strangers escalates the discomfort effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Who's to say we didn't put that very same poison in the drinking water?...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's lying. He doesn't have any poison...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, I don't have any on me. But I do keep some in my fridge at home in the relish jar.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Now see, you look very different from what I remember.' Art Sloan: 'Do I know you people?'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to act as if he and Art Sloan have a longstanding rivalry
jokes.punchline: Art has no idea who they are — the 'rivalry' exists entirely in the gang's heads
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke. The gang's inflated sense of their own importance to others is punctured immediately. Art Sloan not knowing them at all is funnier than any confrontational response would be.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: There's poison in that jar? I thought I was allergic to pickles.

jokes.text: Mac to Art Sloan: 'Flip cup. Ten years ago? We poisoned you, dude. Remember?'
jokes.setup: Art Sloan asks who they are
jokes.punchline: Mac's conversational, casual reminder that they poisoned him — as if this is a perfectly normal thing to bring up as an icebreaker
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and character work. The casual delivery of 'We poisoned you, dude. Remember?' as a conversation-starter is perfectly dark. It assumes shared social memory of a genuinely terrible act, treating it like a fun shared experience. The deadpan is essential — if it were played big, it wouldn't work. Very high craft for how little it uses.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's in the jar with the skull and crossbones?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, that's mayonnaise. That's a decoy. And the mayo? That's shampoo.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I do keep some in my fridge at home in the relish jar.' Charlie: 'There's poison in that jar? I thought I was allergic to pickles.'
jokes.setup: Frank claims to have poison at home, implying a threat
jokes.punchline: Charlie has been unknowingly eating from the poison jar, thinking he had a pickle allergy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The layers are excellent: (1) Frank casually keeps poison in his fridge, (2) it's in the relish jar, (3) Charlie has been eating it, (4) Charlie's self-diagnosis was a pickle allergy. Each layer adds to the absurdity. It's perfect character work for both Frank (casual dangerousness) and Charlie (naive, medically confused). The structure is airtight and the revelation lands with genuine surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're telling me I've been putting shampoo on my sandwiches?

jokes.text: Frank: 'What's in the jar with the skull and crossbones?' 'Oh, that's mayonnaise. That's a decoy.' 'And the mayo?' 'That's shampoo.' Charlie: 'You're telling me I've been putting shampoo on my sandwiches?'
jokes.setup: Following the poison/pickle revelation, we learn Frank's fridge is a labyrinth of mislabeled danger
jokes.punchline: The skull-and-crossbones jar is mayonnaise. The mayo jar is shampoo. Charlie has been eating shampoo sandwiches.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak, and legitimately one of the great Always Sunny bits. The escalating mislabeling system is a perfect absurdist structure: each layer reveals Frank has constructed an elaborate system of deception in his own fridge for no discernible reason, and Charlie has been silently suffering the consequences. 'You're telling me I've been putting shampoo on my sandwiches?' is a legitimately iconic Charlie line. The image of Charlie eating shampoo sandwiches while believing he has a pickle allergy is exactly the kind of deeply sad, perfectly constructed absurdism the show does best. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its escalating specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We came to tell you we're reigniting the rivalry, dick worm.

jokes.text: Mac to Art Sloan: 'Yeah! We came to tell you we're reigniting the rivalry, dick worm.'
jokes.setup: Art asks if there's something he can do for them
jokes.punchline: 'Dick worm' as a casual insult tacked onto a rivalry declaration is a perfectly absurd Mac-ism
jokes.explanation: 'Dick worm' is a great insult invention — specific enough to be memorable, juvenile enough to fit Mac perfectly. The casual delivery selling it as a serious rivalry declaration is good character work.

dialogue.line: Mac urinating on Art's bar after being called childish

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, yeah? How's this for childish, bro?' — followed by him urinating on the bar
jokes.setup: Art Sloan calls the gang childish for the chanting
jokes.punchline: Mac responds to being called childish by urinating on Art's bar
jokes.explanation: The setup is perfect — Art calls them childish, Mac proves him right in the most extreme way possible. The escalation from mild confrontation to public urination is a great Always Sunny move. Followed immediately by Dennis cheering 'He pissed on your bar!' which makes it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Your mother had to have a C-section because of those hands.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'He pissed on your bar! Yeah, call the cops!' — said approvingly, to Art Sloan
jokes.setup: Art Sloan threatens to call the cops after Mac urinates on the bar
jokes.punchline: Dennis enthusiastically encourages Art to call the police, as if this helps their case
jokes.explanation: Dennis confirming 'He pissed on your bar!' as if reporting a fun fact, then agreeing to call the cops with zero self-awareness, is good character work. His obliviousness to self-incrimination is very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Maybe you could be, um, team instigator...

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'll instigate.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Your mother had to have a C-section because of those hands.'
jokes.setup: Dee denies having bison fingers
jokes.punchline: Mac escalates the insult to claim her hands were so large at birth they necessitated a C-section — a completely invented, medically absurd claim delivered as fact
jokes.explanation: The C-section-for-hands joke is a great escalation — it takes the insult into medical absurdity with complete conviction. The specificity (C-section, not just 'your hands are big') gives it real comedic texture.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That was, like, 15 years ago. I don't think you'd have any clout there...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It doesn't matter, man. I was the king of that place. I'm a legend over there.

jokes.text: Frank: 'That's it. She's off the team.' Dee: 'Shut up, Frank!' Mac: 'You're not even on the team!' Frank: 'That's true. What is my role here?'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to assert authority by cutting Dee from the team
jokes.punchline: He's reminded he's not on the team either, then genuinely can't answer what his role is
jokes.explanation: The existential 'What is my role here?' from Frank — with no apparent irony — is perfectly in character. Frank constantly inserts himself into situations where he has no place. The beat of genuine confusion is good.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I chug dick? No. What? I never- I don't chug dick. That's crazy.

jokes.text: Mac designates Frank as 'team instigator' and Frank immediately accepts with enthusiasm: 'I'll be the instigator. Sure. Yeah. Okay. I'll instigate.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs a role that keeps him occupied and away from the actual flip cup
jokes.punchline: Frank accepts 'team instigator' as a completely legitimate and important position, repeating it to himself as if memorizing a job title
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat. Frank's earnest acceptance of a made-up title is consistent with his pathetic need for inclusion. The triple repetition 'I'll instigate' is a good Frank moment.

dialogue.speaker: Frat student
dialogue.line: Dude, we were cruising in sixth grade in '98, man.

jokes.text: Mac's challenge to Dee: flip 10 cups in a row under pressure. Mac to Dennis after Dee leaves: 'That oughta keep her busy for at least a week or so. I don't think she'll ever get that.'
jokes.setup: Mac ostensibly gives Dee a chance to earn her spot back
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals to Dennis it's a task designed to keep her busy and away from the team permanently
jokes.explanation: Classic gang cruelty — a fake chance given purely to manage Dee. The aside to Dennis is a good structural move, letting the audience in on the manipulation.

dialogue.line: Oh, he's a pledge. And we're zapping his nuts with a stun gun every couple of hours.

jokes.text: Dennis claims he's a 'legend' at his old frat, was 'king of that place.' Cut to him arriving and seeing his photo defaced with 'I chug dick' written across it.
jokes.setup: Dennis builds himself up as a legendary frat figure whose legacy endures
jokes.punchline: His alumni photo is defaced with 'I chug dick' — his legacy is exactly the opposite of what he imagined
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff on Dennis's self-aggrandizement. The setup is his confident boasting; the punchline is visual and immediate. The specific vandalism ('I chug dick') rather than something generic makes it funnier. Dennis's indignant reaction — 'That's homophobic. What the hell?' — adds an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, man! You got any ludes?

dialogue.speaker: Frat student
dialogue.line: Ludes? I don't think they make those anymore, man.

jokes.text: Dennis's response to 'I chug dick' being written on his photo: 'Come on, that's homophobic. I mean, come on. What the hell?'
jokes.setup: Dennis sees his defaced photo
jokes.punchline: His objection is on homophobia grounds, not denial — suggesting he's more upset about the slur than the content, which is a very specific and funny deflection
jokes.explanation: Dennis's specific objection to the word choice rather than a denial is a good character beat — it implies he might not entirely disagree with the content, just the framing. Very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't do that shit again, you little idiot! Have some respect for a brother, okay? I'm a legend around this place.

jokes.text: Frank is discovered in the frat house already coaching pledges: 'Bitch! Pick it back up! No, shake the ass! Shake the ass!'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie arrive at the frat to recruit for the flip cup team
jokes.punchline: Frank is already there, deeply embedded in a raunchy frat hazing scenario, completely at home
jokes.explanation: Frank appearing already integrated into the worst of frat culture before Dennis even arrives is a great character moment. His comfort in this environment — 'I almost got this, Dennis' — is perfectly Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frat student
dialogue.line: Flip cup? What are you, a freshman? That is so lame.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm Brother Reynolds, class of '98.' Frat guy: 'Dude, we were cruising in sixth grade in '98, man.'
jokes.setup: Dennis introduces himself as a fraternity brother to establish credibility
jokes.punchline: The current members were 12 years old in 1998, making Dennis's status completely irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured deflation. Dennis's authority claim is immediately nullified by the generational gap. The 'cruising in sixth grade' specificity makes it funnier than just 'we were kids.'

dialogue.line: Dennis and Frank's drug-fueled rant about the disrespectful frat kids

jokes.text: Frat guy: 'Oh, he's a pledge. And we're zapping his nuts with a stun gun every couple of hours.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks what's going on with a struggling pledge
jokes.punchline: Delivered completely casually, as if the nut-zapping schedule is perfectly normal and expected
jokes.explanation: The casualness is the joke. 'Every couple of hours' implies a schedule, a system, oversight — the bureaucratic regularity of testicle electrocution. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, in that movie, Matt Damon played a genius janitor. You're just a janitor.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'That's brutal, man. Wow. Let me... Let me get in on that.'
jokes.setup: Dennis expresses horror at the stun gun hazing
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks to participate
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis character beat. The micro-beat of feigned disgust before genuine enthusiasm is classic Dennis Reynolds — he pretends briefly to be a normal person before his true nature surfaces. The speed of the pivot is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Right. You stumped me with that one. That's a good point.

jokes.text: Dennis gets zapped in the nuts, falls down. Frank: 'Dennis, these guys are badass shitheads! Oh, man! You got any ludes?'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks to participate in the stun gun hazing
jokes.punchline: He gets immediately zapped himself and goes down; Frank's delighted assessment and drug request follow
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on Dennis volunteering. 'Badass shitheads' as Frank's highest compliment is perfect Frank. His immediate pivot to asking for ludes is very character-consistent — he's delighted and wants to maximize the experience.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Or I'd take a banana and stick it up some guy's ass in front of his best friend. And I'd be like, 'Hey! Banana ass! How you doing?'

jokes.text: Frank: 'You got any ludes?' Frat Guy: 'I don't think they make those anymore, man.' Frank: 'No?' — genuinely surprised
jokes.setup: Frank asks for Quaaludes as naturally as asking for a beer
jokes.punchline: He genuinely didn't know ludes had been discontinued, suggesting he was looking for them in earnest
jokes.explanation: Frank's surprise that ludes no longer exist is a great character detail — it speaks to his arrested development and the era he's really living in. The 'No?' lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Or maybe I'd, like, uh- I'd like take the tip of my penis and stick it in a guy's mouth for, like, just a second, you know what I mean? Like while he was sleeping.

jokes.text: Frat guy: 'We got Ritarall.' Frank: 'Ritarall? What's Ritarall?' Frat Guy: 'Oh, snortski.' Frank: 'Ooh! Ooh, that's tasty stuff.'
jokes.setup: Frank can't get ludes but is offered an alternative drug
jokes.punchline: 'Ritarall' (clearly Ritalin/Adderall snorted) introduced as a novelty, and Frank's immediate snort and gustatory approval — 'tasty stuff' — suggests he's essentially a drug garbage disposal
jokes.explanation: 'Ritarall' is a funny portmanteau and 'snortski' is a great casual drug-culture word. 'Ooh, that's tasty stuff' as Frank's reaction to snorting amphetamines is excellent character work — he treats drugs like appetizers.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, what I'm doing is I'm cutting the shower curtain in half waist high so that when he's in using it, people can see his junk.

jokes.text: Frank gets zapped by the stun gun after asking them to do it again
jokes.setup: Frank on Ritarall, surrounded by frat bros, is in his element
jokes.punchline: He asks them to zap him again and they comply — Frank's total embrace of the worst possible environment
jokes.explanation: More of the same stun gun gag. Funny in concept but the third iteration diminishes returns. The joke is now Frank's enthusiasm rather than the act itself.

dialogue.speaker: College girl
dialogue.line: When we shower together and wash each other off.

jokes.text: Dennis after getting zapped again: 'Okay? Have some respect for a brother, okay? I'm a legend around this place. So don't zap me again!'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been repeatedly zapped
jokes.punchline: He invokes his legendary status while also just having been electrocuted in the genitals — his dignity claims are completely unearned in context
jokes.explanation: Decent Dennis moment — the gap between his self-perception (legend) and his reality (just got tasered) is classic Dennis. Diminishing returns on the legend claim gag though.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh! Bet you're reading a lot of Gordon Wood, huh! You read your Gordon Wood and you regurgitate it from a textbook and you think you're wicked awesome doing that!

jokes.text: Frat guys mock Dennis for suggesting flip cup: 'Flip cup? What are you, a freshman? That is so lame. Take a look at how loose his jeans are.'
jokes.setup: Dennis finally tries to pitch the reason he came — flip cup recruitment
jokes.punchline: He gets instantly roasted, with the jeans insult being the final indignity
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'that's lame' to 'his jeans are too loose' is a good deflation sequence. The jeans callback is a nice touch connecting to the opening Frank skinny jeans gag thematically.

dialogue.speaker: Frat student
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about. You are an idiot.

jokes.text: Dee struggling alone with flip cups while grinding her teeth; Dennis: 'Oh, Dee. Dee, it's getting hard to watch. Really. I can't stop grinding my teeth.'
jokes.setup: Dee is practicing flip cups alone obsessively
jokes.punchline: Dennis's teeth-grinding reaction mirrors the painful awkwardness of watching her fail — he's suffering for her
jokes.explanation: The grinding teeth detail is a funny specific reaction. Dennis watching Dee's struggle with physical discomfort rather than pity is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm doing this jerk-off's taxes! Next year the I.R.S. Will audit the piss out of him!

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I don't know how these kids study on this goddamn Ritarall.' Then immediately: 'Yeah, I don't know either! And I don't give a shit!'
jokes.setup: Dennis is apparently on Ritarall himself now
jokes.punchline: He and Dee are both screaming; the drug has clearly affected him and he's shouting non-sequiturs
jokes.explanation: The Ritarall affecting Dennis's behavior is a good continuity gag. 'I don't give a shit' as a response to his own question works.

dialogue.line: Frank creating a poop swastika on Art's lawn

jokes.text: Dennis and Frank's mutual rant about frat kids being 'savages' and 'idiots' who have 'no respect' — while having just asked to participate in stun gun hazing and snorted drugs with them
jokes.setup: Dennis and Frank complain about the disrespectful, savage frat kids
jokes.punchline: They are describing their own behavior exactly — they did everything they're criticizing, and worse
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny irony structure — the gang complaining about behavior they just engaged in. The rant goes on a bit long but the core irony is solid. 'They live in a fantasy world with no consequences for their actions' is a perfect self-description.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: if I had known college was anything like that, the amount of book learning I would have put to my brain- Read! And math, dude!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Yeah, in that movie, Matt Damon played a genius janitor. You're just a janitor.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains his Good Will Hunting plan
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out the obvious flaw — Matt Damon was a genius, Dennis is just a regular janitor — with no malice, just clarity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The structure is perfect — it identifies exactly what's wrong with Dennis's logic in the fewest possible words. Charlie's delivery as a matter-of-fact observation rather than a diss makes it funnier. 'You're just a janitor' is devastating and memorable. High quotability and rewatchability.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Goddamn it. This feels forced. I... I'm not into it. I'm definitely forcing it.

jokes.text: Long pause after Charlie's 'you're just a janitor' line. Dennis: 'Right... You stumped me with that one. That's a good point. You didn't have a comeback for that.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just destroyed Dennis's plan with one sentence
jokes.punchline: Dennis audibly processes being stumped, narrates his own stumping, and then tries to pivot by saying Dennis won't have comebacks either — but Dennis just admitted he had none
jokes.explanation: Good beat following the Charlie line. Dennis narrating his own stumping is very Dennis — he can't just be silent, he has to process it aloud and try to regain control, which makes it worse.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, what's going on is that you just drank a cup of poison! Paddy's Pub, bitches!

jokes.text: Charlie and Dennis arriving at a full-blown paint party, painted women everywhere. Charlie: 'Is this what college is like, man? I don't know, man. I wish I went to college. I feel like I got boned big-time, dude!'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis go back to the frat to 'handle' the situation
jokes.punchline: They walk into what appears to be a spectacular party and Charlie's immediate reaction is wistful regret about not attending college
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sincere lament about missing college — framed entirely around the existence of paint parties — is a good character moment. 'I got boned big-time, dude' is a solid Charlie line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I thought you guys believed in me. You were so proud of me...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, no. We knew you were gonna choke.

jokes.text: Two painted women ask Charlie and Dennis if they want to be painted. Both immediately agree, completely abandoning their purpose.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis just told each other 'Nothing will distract us. Nothing!'
jokes.punchline: Two seconds later, women ask if they want to be painted and they immediately capitulate
jokes.explanation: The 'nothing will distract us / distracted immediately' structure is a classic comedy beat. The setup and payoff are tight and the deflation is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I thought you guys believed in me. You were so proud of me.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, no. We knew you were gonna choke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah. Yeah. We knew you'd pretty much choke under pressure.

jokes.text: Charlie and Dennis getting painted — negotiating the exact process with the women in the most earnest way possible: 'Well, first we paint you, and then you paint us.' 'Well, that makes sense. Sure.'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis are being invited into a paint party
jokes.punchline: Their complete over-analysis of the painting protocol while trying to remain casually cool is both pathetic and charming
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe beat. The earnestness of negotiating painting terms is mildly funny but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Frank's confessional about past hazing: 'I used to dress guys up like bananas and walk them around the quad. Or I'd take a banana and stick it up some guy's ass in front of his best friend.'
jokes.setup: Frank is reminiscing about his own frat days while watching the current frat behavior
jokes.punchline: His hazing memories escalate from dressing as bananas to immediate anal violation — with no tonal shift
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank revelation — delivered as fond nostalgia, the pivot from 'banana costumes' to immediate sexual assault with a banana is pure Frank. 'Hey! Banana ass! How you doing?' as his hazing catchphrase is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank struggling with skinny jeans - can't remove them, no circulation

jokes.text: Frank: 'Or maybe I'd, like, take the tip of my penis and stick it in a guy's mouth for, like, just a second, you know what I mean? Like while he was sleeping.'
jokes.setup: Frank is cataloguing his hazing greatest hits
jokes.punchline: The escalation from banana-based hazing to direct sexual assault, described with casual specificity ('just the tip,' 'while he was sleeping') and framed as the natural next step in the sequence
jokes.explanation: Very dark. Works as character comedy because Frank treats this as equivalent to any other prank. The 'just for a second' qualifier and 'while he was sleeping' detail are delivered with complete sincerity. This is the show at its most transgressive — it works because Frank's obliviousness to the horror of what he's describing is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, Flipadelphia! Oh, sh... Was that today?

jokes.text: Frank: 'But you don't stun gun a guy who was a goddamn legend!' — his conclusion after cataloguing sexual assaults
jokes.setup: Frank has just described increasingly serious sexual violence as hazing pranks
jokes.punchline: His moral conclusion is not about the assaults themselves but about the indignity of being stun-gunned as a legend
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The punchline reframes everything — after describing genuinely horrifying acts with pride, Frank's objection is not to the content but to being treated as anything less than a legend. The moral inversion is perfectly Frank and the economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, Flipadelphia! Oh, sh... Was that today? Yeah, dude.

jokes.text: Frank's rant about frat kids having no respect: 'They live in a fantasy world where there are no consequences for their actions. And I don't understand that.' — said by the man who just described assaulting sleeping people
jokes.setup: Frank is disgusted by the frat kids' behavior
jokes.punchline: His critique of 'no consequences for their actions' is a perfect self-description delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The irony is sharp — Frank is literally the embodiment of everything he's complaining about. Best deployed immediately after the sexual assault hazing catalogue.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I am a legend.

jokes.text: Frank: 'What I'm doing is I'm cutting the shower curtain in half waist-high so that when he's in using it, people can see his junk.'
jokes.setup: Frank is talking about consequences and respect while simultaneously hatching a revenge plot
jokes.punchline: While delivering a lecture about responsibility, Frank is literally preparing a prank to expose someone's genitals
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic juxtaposition — Frank complaining about childishness while doing something childish. The shower curtain half-cut is a specifically conceived prank that shows real thought put into humiliation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Who slams a door? Babies. That guy's got some real growing up to do. I mean, have some respect, for Christ's sake. Goddamn savage. I am a legend.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Wow, Frank. That Ritarall's having a very interesting effect on what you think.' Frank: 'I love this feeling!'
jokes.setup: Frank is cutting shower curtains and planning revenge while monologuing
jokes.punchline: Dennis identifies the drug as the cause; Frank confirms with total enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation on the Ritarall subplot. 'I love this feeling!' after all the chaos he's caused is a good Frank button.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Got any more of it?' Dennis: 'Does a bear shit in the woods?' — then immediately cuts rails
jokes.setup: Frank wants more Ritarall
jokes.punchline: Dennis, who was complaining about the drug moments ago and doesn't 'know how kids study on this,' immediately offers to cut rails
jokes.explanation: Good hypocrisy beat — Dennis was the voice of mild concern and immediately reveals he has more. The classic idiom deployed casually about drug use is funny.

jokes.text: Cut to: Charlie and Dennis fully painted, showering with the women. 'That was awesome.' 'Oh, that's so awesome. And now you do us.' 'Oh, man!' 'And then for the best part...' 'There's a better part than this?'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis were supposed to recruit for flip cup
jokes.punchline: They are now fully painted and in a communal shower with women, with an even better activity promised — they have completely abandoned the mission
jokes.explanation: Good escalation payoff on the paint party subplot. 'There can't be a better part' from Dennis shows he's completely lost to this experience. The shower development is a good escalation step.

jokes.text: Frat guy kicks Charlie and Dennis out: 'You're not in the frat. Get out!' Charlie: 'Guys, you're killing me.'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis are having the time of their lives at the paint party
jokes.punchline: They're immediately ejected because they're not members — back to being losers
jokes.explanation: Expected but satisfying deflation. 'You're killing me' from Charlie, still covered in paint, is a good tag.

jokes.text: Charlie's Good Will Hunting attempt: 'What's your major, dude?' 'Economics.' 'Oh! Bet you're reading a lot of Gordon Wood, huh! You read your Gordon Wood and you regurgitate it from a textbook and you think you're wicked awesome doing that! And how about them apples! And all that Gordon Wood business!'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to pull the Good Will Hunting move on a frat kid
jokes.punchline: His entire arsenal is 'Gordon Wood' (the actual film reference) repeated over and over with increasing desperation, clearly never understanding economics or Gordon Wood himself
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a great character moment. Charlie has taken the GWH plan and his sole implement is 'Gordon Wood' — repeated with increasing volume and decreasing coherence. 'And all that Gordon Wood business!' is a perfect Charlie-ism. The joke perfectly captures Charlie's confident deployment of half-understood knowledge. High quotability — this is a classic Always Sunny moment. The delivery of 'wicked awesome' as a Boston affect he's absorbed from the film is a great detail.

jokes.text: Frat guy: 'I have no idea what you're talking about. You are an idiot.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's Gordon Wood monologue
jokes.punchline: Complete flat dismissal — not even an attempt to engage
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man button on the Gordon Wood rant. The deadpan 'you are an idiot' as the final word is the ideal response.

jokes.text: Frank reveal: 'I'm doing this jerk-off's taxes! Next year the I.R.S. will audit the piss out of him!'
jokes.setup: Frank has been off-screen, presumably plotting revenge on the frat
jokes.punchline: His revenge scheme is fraudulent tax filing — a completely unexpected, long-term bureaucratic attack
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The reveal that Frank is doing someone's taxes as revenge is completely unexpected and perfectly Frank. The layers: (1) Frank knows how to do taxes, (2) he's doing them wrong on purpose, (3) this is how his brain works when on Ritarall, (4) the revenge is delayed — 'next year.' Dennis's reaction 'That's so weird! That's long-term shit!' perfectly voices the audience's reaction. This joke shows genuine comedic originality and character specificity — only Frank Reynolds would think of fraudulent tax filing as frat-house revenge. Comparable to the GWH Gordon Wood payoff as the episode's comedic peak.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Do me a favor, man. Can you go upstairs and look down onto the lawn? I've done it. I've done something.' Dennis: 'You've done it?' Frank: 'Yeah. Give me the cigar. I need that.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been off doing something mysterious
jokes.punchline: He's done 'it' — something so significant he needs a cigar — but we don't know what yet
jokes.explanation: Good buildup joke. Frank's self-satisfaction and the cigar request establish expectation for a big visual reveal.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I've created a masterpiece.' — reveal of what he's done to the lawn (the 'masterpiece')
jokes.setup: Frank has been building to a 'masterpiece' on the frat lawn
jokes.punchline: Whatever Frank has done to the lawn — presumably something deeply inappropriate involving feces, the word 'masterpiece' applied to something horrible — played as a visual reveal
jokes.explanation: The 'masterpiece' reveal (likely a defecation-based installation given context clues and show history) earns its impact through buildup. Frank's pride — 'I think our work here is done' — is classic. The visual joke lives or dies on the actual image, but the structure is solid.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I think our work here is done.' — after the masterpiece reveal
jokes.setup: Frank has just defiled the frat lawn
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'work here is done' as if he's completed a dignified mission
jokes.explanation: Good button on the masterpiece sequence. The deadpan 'work here is done' adds dignity to something undignified.

jokes.text: Charlie and Dennis, still covered in paint, lament not going to college. Charlie: 'I mean, like, if I had known college was anything like that, the amount of book learning I would have put to my brain... Read! And math, dude!'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis reflect on their frat experience
jokes.punchline: Charlie's motivation for academic achievement would have been entirely paint parties and showering with women — 'book learning' is a means to that end, not an end in itself
jokes.explanation: 'Read! And math, dude!' as Charlie's academic aspiration is a great Charlie line — the syntax is broken, the motivation is entirely hedonistic, but there's genuine regret there. Good character work.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'They shower together! And naked!'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dennis are reflecting on the frat party
jokes.punchline: Dennis's specific observation about the shower being both together AND naked — as if one of these details might not be true
jokes.explanation: The 'and naked' specification is a funny redundancy — the logical implication of showering is that you're naked, but Dennis feels the need to confirm it. His delivery of it as a revelation is good.

jokes.text: Art Sloan bursts in with 'Boom! The rivalry's back on!' The gang responds with muted 'Rivalry... Rivalry...' chanting, visibly deflated
jokes.setup: The gang has moved on from Art Sloan and found a new rival
jokes.punchline: Art Sloan has finally committed to the rivalry they no longer want — perfect comic reversal
jokes.explanation: Great structural reversal. The entire episode has been about getting Art Sloan to accept the rivalry, and the moment he does, the gang has moved on. The muted, obligatory 'Rivalry... rivalry...' chant from the gang is a perfect deflation of their earlier enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Goddamn it. This feels forced. I'm definitely forcing it. Something's off!'
jokes.setup: The gang is half-heartedly chanting 'rivalry' with Art Sloan
jokes.punchline: Mac explicitly diagnoses the scene as 'forced' — a meta-commentary on a sitcom rivalry that has lost its momentum
jokes.explanation: Good meta joke. Mac calling out the forced quality of their own rivalry is both a character moment and a commentary on how rivalries work in narrative. 'I'm definitely forcing it' is an unusually self-aware moment for Mac.

jokes.text: Mac: 'They burned me and I haven't let it go.' — still covered in paint
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining why the Art Sloan rivalry feels wrong now
jokes.punchline: Mac's admission that the frat kids 'burned' him — while literally covered in paint from the frat party — is both figurative and potentially literal
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. The visual of Mac still painted while talking about being 'burned' adds texture.

jokes.text: Dee demonstrates flipping 10 cups in a row perfectly, everyone goes nuts. Dennis: 'Holy shit! That was amazing, Dee!'
jokes.setup: Everyone assumed Dee could never flip 10 cups in a row
jokes.punchline: She does it perfectly — earning genuine respect from the gang who made her practice obsessively
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff. Dee earning genuine admiration from the gang who've been cruel to her all episode creates a moment of real tension before the inevitable betrayal. Sets up the poisoning ending perfectly.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I think with Dee's newfound flip cup skills, we can embarrass the shit out of those little bitches!' Dennis: 'I'll tell you what. I will take any excuse to get back to that party.'
jokes.setup: The gang shifts their rivalry to the frat kids
jokes.punchline: Dennis's honesty — his only motivation is getting back to the paint party — undercuts any competitive pretense
jokes.explanation: Dennis's honest admission about the paint party is good character work. The gang's real motivations are always more self-interested than they pretend.

jokes.text: The gang's terms for winning: 'If we win, we get to come to your frat whenever we want.' Charlie: 'And paint girls!' Dennis: 'And get painted by them!' Mac: 'And take showers with them! Lots of showers.'
jokes.setup: The gang proposes the stakes for the flip cup challenge
jokes.punchline: Their 'prize' is entirely about accessing the paint party — their rivalry with the frat is transparently just an excuse to get back in
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the paint party obsession. The escalating specificity — paint girls / get painted / showers, lots of showers — lands well. Mac's 'lots of showers' emphasis is funny.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Frank, you want to start us off with some kind of cheer?' Frank: 'Yeah, that's a good idea. Paddy's! Paddy's! Paddy's!'
jokes.setup: The gang prepares for the big flip cup showdown
jokes.punchline: Frank's cheer is just the bar's name repeated three times — the least inspiring pep talk possible
jokes.explanation: Frank as team instigator delivering the most minimal possible cheer is a good Frank moment. The simplicity is the joke.

jokes.text: During the flip cup tournament, Dee struggles and the gang screams contradictory coaching: 'Too hard! You're hitting yourself in the head.' 'Come on, Dee! Ease up on it, Dee!'
jokes.setup: Dee is supposed to prove herself in the high-stakes moment
jokes.punchline: She's apparently hitting herself in the head with the cup while the gang screams useless instructions
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation. The detail of Dee hitting herself in the head with the cup is very specific physical comedy, and the gang's contradictory yelling ('ease up / come on!') adds to the chaos.

jokes.text: The gang loses. Dee: 'You guys, I'm sorry. You guys, one more time.' Mac: 'Don't you see, Dee? We've already won.'
jokes.setup: The gang loses the flip cup tournament catastrophically
jokes.punchline: 'We've already won' — implying a plan is in motion
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the poison reveal. Mac's cryptic 'we've already won' is delivered with just the right amount of dark smugness.

jokes.text: Revelation: The gang poisoned the frat kids' beer. Mac: 'That was the only way we could beat these little bitches!' Dee: 'I thought you guys believed in me.' Mac: 'Oh, no. We knew you were gonna choke. Yeah. We knew you'd pretty much choke under pressure. Which is why... We poisoned your ass!'
jokes.setup: Dee thought the gang believed in her newfound flip cup skills
jokes.punchline: They never believed in her — they poisoned the opponents because they always knew she'd fail. The poison callback from the episode's opening is now the resolution.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural moments. The poisoning is a full-episode callback, the gang's cruelty to Dee reaches its apex (they performed pride and belief in her entirely as a cover for the poisoning), and Dee's devastated 'I thought you guys believed in me' makes it genuinely dark. The structure — setup the poisoning in scene 1, make the audience forget it, deliver it as the climactic twist — is excellent Always Sunny craft. 'We poisoned your ass' as the punchline to Dee's earnest emotional moment is exactly the show's voice.

jokes.text: The gang celebrates with 'Flip, flip, Flipadelphia!' chant as the frat kids collapse from poisoning
jokes.setup: The frat kids are being poisoned
jokes.punchline: The joyful Flipadelphia chant plays over the scene of people collapsing — the episode's triumphant theme song for a genuinely terrible victory
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal deployment of the running gag. The chant has been used throughout as a marker of enthusiasm; here it plays as a victory song over a poisoning, which makes it both funny and genuinely dark. The juxtaposition is exactly what Always Sunny excels at.

jokes.text: Frank can't get his skinny jeans off. 'They're not coming off! Yank 'em! Yank 'em! We're gonna have to burn 'em off, I think. No! Gotta get 'em off 'cause I got no circulation in my legs.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been wearing his skinny jeans all episode
jokes.punchline: The pants have cut off circulation and must be burned off — the opening vanity gag becomes a medical emergency
jokes.explanation: Great full-episode callback payoff. The skinny jeans gag opened the episode and now closes it with an escalated consequence — circulation loss and potential immolation. 'We're gonna have to burn 'em off' as a serious suggestion is excellent Frank. The structure of opening with vanity and closing with medical emergency is very solid.

jokes.text: Art Sloan confronts the gang about everything they did: 'You disrespected my business. You vandalized my home. All in the name of some stupid drinking competition.' And then when he finally gave in — they didn't even show up.
jokes.setup: Art Sloan has been manipulated, harassed, and had his bar urinated on all episode
jokes.punchline: The gang missed Flipadelphia entirely — the event they destroyed someone's business to participate in — and must be reminded it happened
jokes.explanation: Good structural irony — the gang's grand rivalry project ended with them not even attending the event. Art Sloan's exasperated summary of their crimes is a good accounting of the episode's damage.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Nah. We've moved on.' Dennis: 'Yeah, I'm over it.' Dee: 'That's gonna be a pass for me too. I don't feel well at all. They poisoned me.' Mac: 'I'm not feeling it either. So that's gonna be a unanimous no from us. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Art Sloan has finally agreed to do Flipadelphia, but the gang no longer wants to
jokes.punchline: They reject the offer with casual collective indifference, including Dee noting she was poisoned and Mac treating it like a business decision
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing irony. The formal language — 'that's gonna be a unanimous no from us. Sorry.' — applied to their childish non-participation after ruining this man's life is perfect Always Sunny. Dee noting she was poisoned as a casual explanation among equals is very dark. Mac's business-meeting cadence is spot-on.

jokes.text: Art Sloan slams the door in frustration. Mac: 'What was that? Totally uncalled for.' Dennis: 'Who slams a door?' Mac: 'Babies.' Dennis: 'That guy's got some real growing up to do.' Mac: 'Goddamn savage.'
jokes.setup: Art Sloan, after being harassed, vandalized, and dismissed, slams a door in frustration
jokes.punchline: The gang — who urinated in his bar, poisoned multiple people, and were on Ritarall all day — lectures him on maturity and calls him a savage
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best closing jokes and a perfect Always Sunny button. The gang's complete lack of self-awareness — calling Art Sloan a 'savage' and saying he has 'growing up to do' after everything they've done — is a textbook example of the show's core thesis: these people have zero insight into their own behavior. The escalating condemnation ('babies' → 'growing up to do' → 'goddamn savage') is well-constructed, and 'I am a legend' as Frank's final addition is a perfect button on his entire arc.

jokes.text: Frank's final line: 'I am a legend.'
jokes.setup: The gang is criticizing Art Sloan for slamming a door
jokes.punchline: Frank's non-sequitur self-affirmation 'I am a legend' — spoken with complete sincerity, completely unasked, as a final declaration
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button. 'I am a legend' as a non-sequitur final declaration — spoken by a man who has just been unable to remove his skinny jeans, done a college kid's taxes wrong for revenge, and snorted drugs — is a beautiful encapsulation of the show's themes. The delivery of it as a confident announcement to no one in particular is exactly right.

tmdb_overview: After being banned for 10 years from a local drinking competition appropriately named "Flipadelphia," the gang tries to reignite their old rivalry with another local bar. Finding that they are in need of some serious practice, the guys head to Dennis' old fraternity house at the University of Pennsylvania to get their game up to speed while Dee hones her skills on her own. Frank wears skinny pants.
